Our room has one desk, so I see everything Vidya does with her essays. Last semester she rewrote one introduction until three in the morning and still handed it in late.

This Sunday was different. At four she put her phone on the shelf, set an alarm for seven and said, "Rukmini, if I'm still fiddling when this rings, take the laptop away." I laughed, but she meant it.

At seven the alarm went. She read the essay once, fixed two commas, and pressed submit. Then she opened a small notebook and wrote three lines. I peeked later: "Next time: start the reading earlier. Shorter quotes. Clearer last paragraph."

She ate dinner with us for the first time in weeks. I can't say she wasn't still thinking about the essay, but she was laughing at our jokes.

qa.a: Vidya set an alarm for seven.

qa.a: Vidya was probably nervous that she would slip back into endless fiddling, so she wanted an outside check to protect the limit she had set.

Kalyani, sit, you're making me nervous with all that pacing. Let me tell you something from when I was your age.

My final-year project was a model bridge. I wanted every joint perfect. Two weeks before the deadline, I still had not glued the deck, because the railings were a millimetre off. My guide, an old professor with chalk on her sleeves, looked at it and said, "Lokesh, you have until Friday evening. Whatever stands on Friday, you submit."

I was furious. But on Friday at five I stopped. The railings were still a little off. The bridge held the test weight anyway, and I passed well. That night I wrote in the back of my file: next time, cut all the parts first, then fix details.

I still have that file. So, how long are you giving your thesis chapter?

Binita's work is the most accurate on this team. Her vendor report this month had no errors at all. It also reached me nine days after the others, and by then the purchase decision had been made using the rough sheet from the procurement team.

I have noticed a pattern. She stays after eight most nights. On Tuesday I saw her redo a table because two columns were not the same width. When I asked about Saturday's team lunch, she said she had "the formatting to finish".

Today I sat with her and asked what "done" looks like for her. She was quiet, then said, "When nobody can find anything wrong." We agreed to try a draft-by-Thursday rule next month, with me reading it for substance only.

I'll check in weekly. She is too good to burn out on column widths.

Lakshmi

The power went out across the colony at eight, and Simran's grant proposal was due at midnight. Pradeep came up the stairs with a torch and found her on the balcony, laptop at eleven percent, rereading the budget table for the twentieth time.

"You cancelled my birthday dinner for this," Pradeep said gently. "Is it nearly done?"

"The table's fine. It's the wording. It sounds clumsy."

"Let me read it as a draft. Just one pass, then you send it before the battery dies."

She hesitated, then turned the screen. By torchlight Pradeep read aloud. Two sentences really were clumsy; they fixed them in five minutes. The rest was solid.

At nine percent Simran pressed submit. She sat back, shaking a little. "I haven't slept properly in a week," she said. Pradeep switched off the torch and they sat in the dark, listening to the generators hum.

I'm Mridul, and this happened over the summer holidays.

At Parveen's farewell party I tried to make a speech. I said, "We'll all miss you, even though you never share your chips." It was meant to be funny. Nobody laughed. Parveen smiled, kind of.

For the next five days I replayed it. Brushing my teeth, on my cycle, during cricket. Each time I added something worse: maybe Parveen cried later, maybe everyone had messaged about it. I kept thinking I was working it out, like a sum. I wasn't. I was just pressing the bruise.

On the sixth day Parveen sent me a voice note from the new city: "Mridul, send the photos from the party!" Totally normal voice.

I felt stupid and relieved at once. Now when a line starts looping, I ask myself: is this solving anything, or just pressing the bruise?

Sarita, you think you're the first one to fail an exam? Come, let me tell you about your Manoj mama.

Second year of engineering, I failed Fluid Mechanics. Thirty-one out of a hundred. I came back to the hostel and lay on the bed and asked the ceiling, why? Why me? Was I stupid? Had my father wasted his money? My roommate Gopal went to dinner, came back, and I was still asking the same questions. For two weeks I did that. I didn't open a single book. I felt worse every day.

Then Gopal threw the question paper on my chest. "Stop asking why. Circle the questions you couldn't do." I circled six. Four were from the same chapter I'd skipped.

That's all. A chapter, not my whole worth. I cleared the supplementary in October. So, Sarita beta, which chapter did you skip?

Mahima caught herself in the shower on Saturday morning, arguing with her sister again in her head about the words at Friday's dinner. She'd had the same argument at midnight, and at three.

She got out, dried her hair and took the small green notebook off the fridge. She wrote: "I'm still hurt about what Madhav said about my job." Then she set the kitchen timer for ten minutes and let herself think about it properly, pen moving.

I'm Ankita, and I used to think turning a problem over all night was being responsible.

Last month my landlord raised the rent and I spent evenings running the same sums in my head, lying on the floor with the fan clicking. I'd get up exhausted.

My friend Rafiq showed me what he does. Now when I catch the loop, I write the worry in one line on a card. I give it twenty minutes at the table with tea, no phone. I actually think: options, costs, who to ask. When the twenty minutes end, I cook something fiddly. Last night it was dosa batter. Grinding it takes all my attention.

It doesn't vanish. But it shrinks. And Rafiq made me promise something too: if it ever gets constant, or dark, I don't try to handle it with cards. I see someone qualified. I've kept a counsellor's number on the fridge, just in case.

qa.a: Last night it was dosa batter.

qa.a: Ankita felt exhausted and trapped in the loop, yet at the time thought turning it over was being responsible.

grounding: An adult describes writing worries down, giving them set time, cooking something absorbing, and keeping professional help ready.

My name is Amandeep. Last year, when I was nine, nights were the worst part of the day.

Tutor's note, Wednesday

Ankita arrived for the physics session and spent the first twenty minutes listing what could go wrong in the board exam: the paper might be set from the other textbook, she might get the numericals wrong, her pen might leak, she might faint in the hall, she might lose her place in the queue for the college she wants. She said, "I have to think of everything, otherwise I'm being careless."

She had not opened the chapter on current electricity since Saturday.

I did not argue with the list. I asked her to pick the one thing on it she could do something about today. She chose numericals. We did six together; she got four right and was surprised.

I've asked her to bring the list next time, and we'll give it five minutes before we study, not forty. I'll also mention to her parents that she's carrying a lot.

Nilesh, physics tutor

I'm Sarita. I never used to check the gas knob. By April I was checking it three times before bed.

It started in March, when Binita didi's final exams began. She'd walk around the flat at night checking the door, the gas, her hall ticket, the alarm. She'd ask me, "Did you lock the balcony?" even when she'd seen me lock it. Her voice was tight all the time.

At first I found it annoying. Then I caught myself doing it too. I began checking my own bag twice for my college ID. I lay awake listening for the door.

One Sunday Mummy sat us both down. She said, "We're all carrying Binita's exam fear. Let's talk about it plainly." Didi admitted she was scared. I admitted I'd started checking too. We made a rule: one check of the gas and the door, by whoever is last to bed, and then we say goodnight. It's lighter now. Mostly.

Counsellor's note, college wellbeing centre

Tanvir, first year, came in today saying he couldn't focus in lectures. As we talked, it emerged that his older brother is preparing for a competitive exam at home and has been very anxious for months: counting study hours aloud, checking the time every few minutes, asking the family to keep phones silent.

Tanvir now does similar things. He showed me his planner with every half hour marked, and said he checks his watch "maybe fifty times a class". He said he felt jumpy at home and felt he wasn't allowed to relax while his brother suffered.

We talked about how worry can travel through a house without anyone meaning it to. I suggested he try saying to his brother, gently, how the tension feels to him, and that the family agree on shared quiet hours and some shared non-study time.

He'll come back next week. I'll follow up.
